label: prop-A
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-A}
	Let $\mathcal{D}$ be an oper on $C$ 
    with $d-2$ simple apparent singularities $x_3, \dots, x_d$, where $d \leq 3g-3$, and let $x_0 \in C$ be generic.
	Then there exists a holomorphic family $\{\mathcal{D}_u\}_{u\in z(U)}$ with $\mathcal{D}_0 = \mathcal{D}$ such that, for $u \neq 0$, $\mathcal{D}_u$ has simple apparent 
    singularities at $x_+(u), x_-(u), x_3, \dots, x_d$, and the accessory parameters of $x_\pm(u)$ with respect to the projective chart $z$ are of the form
	\[ \nu_\pm(u) = \pm \frac{3}{4u} + \mathcal{O}(u). \]
	(See \Cref{prop-bb-limit-3}; the precise form of $\nu_\pm(u)$ is \eqref{eqn-form-B}.)

name: Reduction of apparent singularities

label: thm-B
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm-B}
	Suppose moreover that $d$ is even and that the projective monodromy of $\mathcal{D}$ is irreducible.
	Then the holomorphic family $\{\mathcal{D}_u\}$ of \Cref{prop-A} is defined by a holomorphic family $\{[E_u, \nabla_u]\}_u$ in $\mathcal{M}_{dR}$ 
	together with line subbundles $L_u \hookrightarrow E_u$ of degree
	\[ \deg L_u = g-1-\frac{d}{2} \quad \text{for } u \neq 0, \qquad \qquad \deg L_0 = g - \frac{d}{2}, \]
	and $D_{L_u}(\nabla_u) = x_+(u) + x_-(u) + x_3 + \dots + x_d$ for $u \neq 0$, $D_{L_0}(\nabla_0) = x_3 + \dots + x_d$.
	For $d < 2g-2$, $[E_u, \nabla_u]$ lies in the partial oper stratum labelled by $d$ for $u \neq 0$, 
	and in the partial oper stratum labelled by $d-2$ at $u = 0$.
	(See \Cref{prop-family-dR,cor-crossing-strata}.)

label: thm-C
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm-C}
	For sufficiently small $u \neq 0$, 
    the branched projective structure corresponding to $\mathcal{D}_u$ of \Cref{prop-A} 
    is the output of a bubbling surgery 
    that creates branch points that correspond to the apparent singularities $x_+(u)$ and $x_-(u)$.
    Specifically, this bubbling surgery takes as an input the branched projective structure $\sigma_u$, 
    which is obtained by removing the bubble bounded by the twin paths and identifying these twin paths, 
    and has simple apparent singularities at $x_3, \dots, x_d$.

title: Definition
body_md:
A projective connection on $C$ is a pair $(P, s)$ where
	$P$ is a flat $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$-bundle on $C$ with $\mathbb{P}^1$-fibers
	and $s: C \rightarrow P$ is a global holomorphic section which is not parallel w.r.t. the flat structure of $P$.
	The points where $ds = 0$ are called apparent singularities;
	the order of an apparent singularity is the order of the zero of $ds$ at that point.

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $N$ be a line bundle on $C$, defined via transition functions $(N)_{\alpha \beta}$ over a coordinate covering $\mathcal{U} = \{ (U_\alpha, z_\alpha) \}_{\alpha \in \mathcal{I}}$ of $C$. 
	An \emph{oper} $\mathcal{D}$ on $N$ for the coordinate covering $\mathcal{U}$ is a collection of meromorphic differential operators $\{ \mathcal{D}_\alpha = \partial_{z_\alpha}^2 + q_\alpha(z_\alpha)\}_{\alpha \in \mathcal{I}}$ 
	such that $f_\alpha(z_\alpha)$ is a solution to $\mathcal{D}_\alpha$ 
	if and only if $(N)_{\beta \alpha} f_\alpha$ is a solution to $\mathcal{D}_\beta \mid_{U_\alpha \cap U_\beta}$. 
	The points at which $\left( \frac{f_{\alpha,1}}{f_{\alpha,2}} \right)' = 0$, where $f_{\alpha,1}$ and $f_{\alpha,2}$ are two linearly independent solutions of $\mathcal{D}_\alpha$, 
	are called apparent singularities,
	with the order of the apparent singularity defined to be the order of the zero of $\left( \frac{f_{\alpha,1}}{f_{\alpha,2}} \right)'$. 
	Two opers on $N$ for two coordinate coverings are considered equivalent if their union is also an oper. 
	An oper on $N$ is an equivalence class of opers on $N$ for different coverings.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
It was shown in \cite{iwasaki91} that an oper exists on a line bundle $N$ if and only if $\deg(N) = 1-g$, 
	such as $N \cong K^{-1/2}$. 
	Such an oper then can be regarded as a differential operator $N \rightarrow N K^2$ whose principal symbol is 1 and subprincipal symbol is 0 \cite{Fr07}.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
On a compact Riemann surface $C$ of genus $g\geq 2$, the most distinguished projective connection is induced by the uniformization theorem, which realizes $C$ as a quotient of the upper-half plane
	and equips on it a distinguished maximal coordinate atlas $\{\left( U_\alpha, x_\alpha \right) \}$ from the upper-half plane.
	We call this the uniformizing projective structure of $C$.
	Since nowhere $dx_\alpha = 0$, the projective structure $\{\left( U_\alpha, x_\alpha \right) \}$ has no apparent singularity. 
	The corresponding oper takes the form $\partial_{x_\alpha}^2$ in each $U_\alpha$. 
	This uniformizing projective structure is distinguished in the sense that the projective coordinates $x_\alpha$ all take values in the upper half-plane.
	
	It follows from \eqref{pre2_SL_operator_transit} that if $q$ is a holomorphic quadratic differential, then $\mathcal{D}_\alpha \coloneqq \partial_{x_\alpha}^2 + q(x_\alpha)$ glue into an oper that has no apparent singularity. 
	These form the space of holomorphic projective connections,
	i.e. those that have no apparent singularities, which is an affine space modeled over $H^0(K^2) \cong \mathbb{C}^{3g-3}$.
	The isomorphism class of each such oper is equivalent
	to a maximal coordinate atlas that is also a projective structure.

title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor-isom-projective-connections}
	Two projective connections 
	with the same irreducible projective monodromy representations up to conjugation
	that have lifts to $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb C)$
	and the same divisors of apparent singularities
	of degree $< 2g-2$
	are isomorphic.

title: Proof
body_md:
Two such projective connections are the projectivization of a holomorphic connection $(F,\nabla)$ and subbundles $L_1$, $L_2$ of $F$ 
	such that $s_{L_1}(\nabla)$, $s_{L_2}(\nabla)$ both vanish at $\mathbf{x}$ and are identified
	via the isomorphism $KL_1^{-2} \cong \mathcal{O}_C(\mathbf{x}) \cong KL_2^{-2}$. 
	But $\deg(\mathbf{x}) < 2g-2$, therefore $L_1$ and $L_2$ destabilize $F$ and must be the same subbundle of $F$.

title: Terminology
body_md:
By \Cref{subsubsec-projective-structures} and the proposition above, a projective structure on $C$ possibly with apparent singularities, an isomorphism class of projective connections, and an oper are equivalent descriptions of the same object, a $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$-oper with apparent singularities in the terminology of \cite{Dinh24}; we simply call it an \emph{oper}, or an \emph{oper with apparent singularities} for emphasis.
When its monodromy lifts to $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb C)$, it is given by data $(L \hookrightarrow F, \nabla)$, up to twisting by a square root of $\mathcal{O}_C$, which we call an \emph{$\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb C)$-oper with apparent singularities}.
We denote it by $\mathcal{D}$ and use its local form $\partial_z^2 + q(z)$ when computing in a local coordinate $z$.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-limit-BA-divisor}
	Let $(E, \phi) \in \mathcal{M}_H$ with 
	associated non-degenerate spectral curve $\widetilde{C} \overset{\pi}{\rightarrow} C$, 
	and $L \hookrightarrow E$ a line subbundle with Baker--Akhiezer divisor $\widetilde{D}$. 
	Let $U \subset C$ be a simply connected open set that contains no branch point of $\widetilde{C}$ and no point of $\mathrm{Nm}(\widetilde{D})$, 
	and let $U' \coloneqq \left\{ (x_+, x_-) \in U^2 \mid  x_+ \neq x_- \right\}$.
	Then there exist a holomorphic family $\{(E_{x_+, x_-}, \phi_{x_+, x_-})\}_{(x_+, x_-) \in U'}$ in $\mathcal{M}_H$ 
	and line subbundles $L_{x_+, x_-} \hookrightarrow E_{x_+, x_-}$ of degree $\deg(L) - 1$, depending holomorphically on $(x_+, x_-)$, 
	such that 
	\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
		\item for all $(x_+, x_-) \in U'$, the Baker--Akhiezer divisor of $(L_{x_+, x_-} \hookrightarrow E_{x_+, x_-}, \phi_{x_+, x_-} )$ is $\widetilde{D} + \tilde{x}_+ + \tilde{x}_-$, 
		where $\tilde{x}_\pm \in \pi^{-1}(x_\pm)$ lie in two fixed distinct components of $\pi^{-1}(U)$; 
		\item for all $x_0 \in U$, 
		$\underset{x_+ \rightarrow x_0 \leftarrow x_-}{\lim} [L_{x_+, x_-}] = [ L(-x_0)]$ in $\mathrm{Pic}^{\deg(L)-1}(C)$
		and $\underset{x_+ \rightarrow x_0 \leftarrow x_-}{\lim}(E_{x_+, x_-}, \phi_{x_+, x_-}) = (E, \phi)$ in $\mathcal{M}_H$.
	\end{enumerate}

	$x_r(x) \neq x$ and $\mathbf{x}^{3g-3}(x)$ is $Q$-generic.

	$\left\{ q^{(i)}_{z, x, \mathbf{x}} \right\}_{x \in U}$

	where $R^{(i)}_{z, x, \mathbf{x}^{3g-3}} (z)$ is the restriction 
	of a holomorphic function $R^{(i)}(z_1, z_2)$ defined on $(U, z) \times (U, z)$
	to the slice $\{ z_1 = z(x), z_2 \equiv z \}$. \\

	$x \mapsto \mathbf{x}^{3g-4}(x) = x_1(x) + ... + x_{3g-4}$,

title: Proof
body_md:
The existence of $\mathcal{D}_0 = \mathcal{D}_{pr} + q_0$ with $q_0$ of the form \eqref{db-limit} follows from
	the definition \eqref{q-u-setup} of $q_u$
	and \Cref{lemma-db-limit-1}.
	Let $q^{reg}_0(z)$ be the regular part on $U$ of $q_0(z)$, i.e.
	\begin{align*}
		&q^{reg}_0(z) \coloneqq q_0(z) - \left(- \frac{2 }{z^2}   + \frac{2 \nu_0 }{z}  \right) dz^2 \nonumber \\
		= &\hspace{3pt} q^{(0)}_0(z)
		+ \left[ 2\nu_0  R^{(1)}_{0}(z)
		-\frac{1}{4} \check{R}^{(1)}(z) 
		- \frac{3}{2}R^{(2)}_0(z) \right]  dz^2
		+  \sum_{r=3}^{d} \nu_r(0) q_{0, x_r}^{(1)} (z) - \frac{3}{4} \sum_{r=3}^{d} q^{(2)}_{0, x_r} (z).
	\end{align*}
	To prove the proposition, it remains to show that the coefficients of the Laurent tail of $q_0(z)$ satisfy the condition making $x_0$ a double apparent singularity, 
	i.e. for $q^{reg}_0(z) =  \sum_{k\geq 0} q_{0, k} z^k$ we have
	\begin{align}\label{db-condition-limit}
		\nu_0^3 + q_{0, 0} \nu_0 + \frac{q_{0,1}}{2} = 0.
	\end{align}
	To this end, for each $u\neq 0$, let $q^{reg}_u(z)$ be the regular part on $U$ of $q_u(z)$, i.e.
	\begin{align*}
		q^{reg}_u(z) 
		&\coloneqq q_u(z) -
		\left( - \frac{3}{4(z-u)^2} - \frac{3}{4(z+u)^2}
		+ \frac{\nu_+(u)}{z-u} + \frac{\nu_-(u)}{z+u} \right)  \nonumber \\
		&= q^{(0)}_u (z)
		+ \sum_{s \in \{\pm\}} \nu_s(u) R^{(1)}_{u,s}(z) 
		- \frac{3}{4} \sum_{s \in \{\pm\}} R^{(2)}_{u,s} (z) 
		+ \sum_{r=3}^{d} \nu_r(u) q_{u, x_r}^{(1)}(z) - \frac{3}{4} \sum_{r=3}^{d} q^{(2)}_{u, x_r} (z).
	\end{align*}
	As a function of both $u$ and $z$, the leading term in $u$ of $q^{reg}_u(z)$ 
	comes from the leading terms in $\nu_\pm(u) R^{(1)}_{u, \pm}(z)$ and is equal to $-(R^{(1)}_{u,+}(z) - R^{(1)}_{u,-}(z) )/( 4u)$.
	By part 2 of \Cref{lemma-linear-system-right-side}, 
	this has a well-defined $u\rightarrow 0$ limit.
	Hence $q^{reg}_u(z)$ has a well-defined $u\rightarrow 0$ limit,
	and in fact $q^{reg}_u(z)  \overset{ u \rightarrow 0}{\longrightarrow} q^{reg}_0(z)$. 
	
	Now, this enables us to expand $q^{reg}_u(z) = \sum_{m, n \geq 0} q_{m,n} u^m z^n$,
	where letting $m=0$ gives the coefficients $q_{0, n}$ of the Taylor expansion $q^{reg}_0(z) =  \sum_{n \geq 0} q_{0, n} z^n$.
	Plugging this expansions of $q^{reg}_0(z)$ and $\nu_{\pm}(u)$ into condition \eqref{SL-operator_residue-constraint-1} for $z = \pm u$, 
	\begin{align*}
		&\nu_\pm(u)^2 - \frac{3}{4} \frac{1}{(2u)^2} + \frac{\nu_\mp(u)}{(\pm 2 u)} + q^{reg}_u(\pm u) = 0,
		&u \neq 0,
	\end{align*}
	we obtain a series of constraints by order of $u$ starting from the order $u^{-2}$.
	The constraints up to order $u^{-1}$ are automatically satisfied by the leading terms of $\nu_\pm(u)$.
	Solving the constraints at order $u^0$ and $u^1$, 
	we obtain \eqref{db-condition-limit}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix a holomorphic projective structure with corresponding oper $\mathcal{D}_{pr}$, 
	and choose coordinate neighborhoods $(U_r, z_r)$ of $x_r$ for $3 \leq r \leq d$ 
	and $(U,z)$ of $x_0$ subordinate to this holomorphic projective structure,
	where $U$ satisfies condition \eqref{condition-neighborhood}.
	We can write $\mathcal{D} = \mathcal{D}_{pr} + q_{\mathcal{D}}$, where $q_\mathcal{D}$ is a meromorphic quadratic differential
	with local expression $-\frac{3}{4(z-z_r(x_r))^2} dz_r^2 + \frac{\nu^\mathcal{D}_r}{z-z_r(x_r)} dz_r^2 + ...$ on $U_{r}$, $3 \leq r \leq d$,
	and $-\frac{2}{z^2} dz^2 + \frac{2 \nu^\mathcal{D}_0}{z} dz^2 + ...$ on $U$.
	Then there exists a unique holomorphic quadratic differential $q^{(0)}_0 (\mathcal{D})$ such that $q_{\mathcal{D}}$ can be written in the form \eqref{db-limit}, i.e.
	\begin{align*}
		q_{\mathcal{D}} = 
		q^{(0)}_0 (\mathcal{D}) + q^{(2)}_{x_0}(\nu^\mathcal{D}_0)
		+  \sum_{r=3}^{d} \nu^\mathcal{D}_r q_{0, x_r}^{(1)} - \frac{3}{4} \sum_{r=3}^{d} q^{(2)}_{0, x_r}.
	\end{align*}
	By \Cref{lemma-tune-limit-hol-q}, there exist holomorphic functions $\nu_3(u)$, ..., $\nu_{d}(u): z(U) \rightarrow \mathbb C$, 
	$\nu_\pm(u): z(U\setminus \{x_0\}) \rightarrow \mathbb C$ with Laurent expansions at $u =0$ of the forms \eqref{eqn-form-D} 
	(in particular, with $\nu_0^\mathcal{D}$ as the coefficient of order $u^0$),
	and a family $\{q^{(0)}_u\}_{u\in z(U)}$ of holomorphic quadratic differentials with $\underset{u \rightarrow 0}{\lim} q^{(0)}_u = q^{(0)}_0 (\mathcal{D})$ such that 
	\begin{align*}
		&q_u = q^{(0)}_u 
		+ \sum_{s\in\{ \pm\}} \nu_{s}(u) q^{(1)}_{u, s}
		- \frac{3}{4} \sum_{s\in \{\pm\}} q^{(2)}_{u, s}
		+ \sum_{r=3}^{d} \nu_r(u) q_{u, x_r}^{(1)} - \frac{3}{4} \sum_{r=3}^{d} q^{(2)}_{u, x_r},
		&u \neq 0,
	\end{align*}
	is a meromorphic quadratic differential with simple apparent singularities at $x_3$, ..., $x_d$ and $x_\pm \in U$ with $z(x_\pm) = \pm u$.
	By \Cref{prop-db-limit-2}, $q_0 \coloneqq \underset{u \rightarrow 0}{\lim} q_u = q_\mathcal{D}$, 
	and hence $\{\mathcal{D}_u \coloneqq \mathcal{D}_{pr} + q_u \}_{u\in z(U)}$ defines a family we seek.
	
	To see that taking the projective monodromy representation 
	of $\mathcal{D}_u$ defines a holomorphic map $U \rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(\pi_1, \mathrm{PSL}_2)$,
	consider a coordinate neighborhood $(V, w)$,
	where $V$ is distinct from $U\cup \{x_3, ..., x_d\}$ and $w$ is subordinate to the chosen holomorphic projective structure.
	On $(V, w)$, $\mathcal{D}_u$ takes the form $\partial_w^2 + q_u(w)$ 
	where $q_u(w)$ is a function holomorphic on $U \times V$.
	By standard results on differential equations that vary holomorphically with respect to deformation parameters \cite{ilyashenko-yakovenko},
	the local solutions to $\partial_w^2 + q_u(w)$ are holomorphic functions on $U \times V$.
	Analytically continuing the ratio of two such linearly independent solutions defines the projective monodromy representation of $\mathcal{D}_u$, 
	which is now holomorphic in $u$.
	By
{ 
\cite[Corollary~5.4]{dinh-thesis} 
} 
, if the number of apparent singularities is less than $2g-2$ to start with, 
	this holomorphic map is injective.

\label{lemma-bb-limit-1}
	Let $x_0$, $x_3$, ..., $x_d$ be distinct points on $C$, 
	$(U,z)$ a coordinate neighborhood of $x_0$ with $z(x_0) = 0$,
	$\nu_{\pm}(u) = \pm \frac{3}{4u} \pm \nu' u + \mathcal{O}(u^2)$ holomorphic functions on $U \setminus \{x_0\}$,

		\sum_{s\in \{\pm\}} \nu_s(u) q^{(1)}_{u, s} - \frac{3}{4} \sum_{s\in \{\pm\}} q^{(2)}_{u, s},
	\end{align}

	extends to a family parameterized by $U$.
	The quadratic differential $\Delta q^{(0)}_{x_0}$ 
	corresponding to the extension to $x_0$
	is holomorphic on $C$,
	vanishes at $x_3$, ..., $x_{d}$,
	and on $U$ takes the form
	\begin{align}\label{delta-q}
		\Delta q^{(0)}_{x_0} = \left[ \frac{3}{4} \check{R}^{(1)}(z) - \frac{3}{2} R^{(2)}_0(z) \right] dz^2.

body_md:
\label{prop-family-dR}
	Let $\{\mathcal{D}_u\}_{u \in z(U)}$ be a family as in \Cref{prop-bb-limit-3} with $d$ even, 
	and suppose that the projective monodromy of $\mathcal{D}_0$ is irreducible.
	Then, after shrinking $U$, there exist a holomorphic family $\{[E_u, \nabla_u]\}_{u \in z(U)}$ in $\mathcal{M}_{dR}$
	and line subbundles $L_u \hookrightarrow E_u$ with $\mathcal{D}_u = \mathcal{D}_{(L_u \hookrightarrow E_u, \nabla_u)}$.
	In particular, for the closed strata \eqref{eqn-closed-strata},
	\[ [E_u, \nabla_u] \in \mathcal{M}^{\leq d}_{dR} \quad \text{for all } u \in z(U), \qquad \qquad [E_0, \nabla_0] \in \mathcal{M}^{\leq d-2}_{dR}. \]

title: Proof
body_md:
As the number of apparent singularities is even throughout the family $\{\mathcal{D}_u\}$, 
	we can lift the projective monodromy $\rho_u$ of $\mathcal{D}_u$ 
	to a holomorphic family $\check{\rho}_u$ of $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb C)$-representations.
	Since $\rho_0$ is irreducible and irreducibility is an open condition, $\check{\rho}_u$ is irreducible for all $u \in z(U)$ after shrinking $U$.
	Since the Riemann--Hilbert correspondence is biholomorphic on irreducible representations \cite{simpson-moduli2}, 
	the flat connections $[E_u, \nabla_u]$ with monodromy $\check{\rho}_u$ form a holomorphic family. 
	Since $(E_u, \nabla_u)$ realizes the monodromy of $\mathcal{D}_u$, the oper $\mathcal{D}_u$ is induced by a line subbundle $L_u \hookrightarrow E_u$, i.e.\ $\mathcal{D}_u = \mathcal{D}_{(L_u \hookrightarrow E_u, \nabla_u)}$ (cf. \Cref{subsec-projective-structures}).
	Note that 
	\[ \deg(L_u^{-2}K) = \deg \mathrm{div}(\mathcal{D}_u) = 
	\begin{cases} 
		d, & u \neq 0, \\ 
		d-2, & u = 0. 
	\end{cases} \]

label: prop-Joukowsky
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-Joukowsky}
	\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
		\item
$J: \mathbb{P}^1 \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^1$ has degree $2$: for $\xi \in \mathbb{C}$, $J(w) = \xi$ if and only if $w^2 - \xi w + 1 = 0$, and $J^{-1}(\infty) = \{0, \infty\}$.
		\item The critical points of $J(w)$ are $w = \pm 1$, and the corresponding critical values are $J(\pm 1) = \pm 2$.
		\item $J(\mathbb{S}^1) = [-2, 2]$ where $\mathbb{S}^1$ is the unit circle.
		\item The restriction of $J$ to $\mathrm{int} (\mathbb{D}_1)$ is a biholomorphism to $\mathbb{P}^1 \setminus [-2, 2]$.
	\end{enumerate}

title: Proposition
body_md:
$J(w)$ is a developing map of the differential equation defined by \eqref{eqn-limit-P1},
	\[ \left( \partial_w^2 - \frac{3}{(w-1)^2 (w+1)^2} \right) f(w) = 0.  \]
	In other words, there exists a basis of solutions $f_1(w)$ and $f_2(w)$ with $J = f_1/f_2$.

title: Proof
body_md:
We have $J' = 1 - w^{-2} = \frac{w^2-1}{w^2}$, $J'' = \frac{2}{w^3}$ and $J''' = -\frac{6}{w^4}$, so that
\[ \frac{J''}{J'} = \frac{2}{w(w^2-1)}, \qquad \frac{J'''}{J'} = -\frac{6}{w^2(w^2-1)}. \]
Hence
\[ \{ J, w \} = \frac{J'''}{J'} - \frac{3}{2} \left( \frac{J''}{J'} \right)^2 
= -\frac{6}{w^2(w^2-1)} - \frac{6}{w^2(w^2-1)^2} 
= -\frac{6}{(w-1)^2(w+1)^2}, \]
i.e.\ $\frac{1}{2}\{J, w\}$ is the potential of \eqref{eqn-limit-P1}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Note that $R > 2$ since $R - R^{-1} > M > 2$.
	For $|w| \geq R$ we have
	\[ |J(w)| = |w + w^{-1}| \geq |w| - |w|^{-1} \geq R - R^{-1} > M,\]
	since $t \mapsto t - t^{-1}$ is increasing.
	Hence $J^{-1}(\overline{\mathbb{D}}_M) \subset \mathbb{D}_R$, and in particular $\overline{\mathcal{A}} \subset \mathbb{D}_R$.
	Since $c(\theta) \geq M^2 - 2 > 2$, we have $\rho > 1$, and so $\overline{\mathcal{H}} \subset \overline{\mathbb{D}}_1 \subset \mathbb{D}_R$.
	Therefore $\overline{\mathcal{B}} = \overline{\mathcal{A}} \cup \overline{\mathcal{H}} \subset \mathbb{D}_R$.

	In other words, for every $\eta > 0$ there is $\tau > 0$ with $d(A_u(w), J(w)) = d(A_u(w), A_0(w)) < \eta$ for all $|u| < \tau$ and $w \in \overline{\mathcal{B}}$.

label: lem-gap
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem-gap}
	Let $0 \leq s < r$, and $a, b \in \mathbb{P}^1$ with $|a| \leq s$ and $|b| \geq r$. Then $d(a, b) \geq d(s, r)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $x = |a|$ and $y = |b|$, so that $x \leq s < r \leq y$.
	If $b = \infty$, then $d(a, b) = 2/\sqrt{1+x^2} \geq 2/\sqrt{1+s^2} > d(s, r)$, since $r - s < \sqrt{1+r^2}$.
	Otherwise $|a - b| \geq y - x > 0$, and $(1+x^2)(1+y^2) = (1+xy)^2 + (y-x)^2$ gives
	\[ d(a, b) \geq \frac{2(y-x)}{\sqrt{(1+xy)^2 + (y-x)^2}} = h\big(\tau(x,y)\big), \qquad 
	\tau(x, y) \coloneqq \frac{y-x}{1+xy}, \qquad h(\tau) \coloneqq \frac{2}{\sqrt{1+\tau^{-2}}}. \]
	Since $h$ is increasing and $d(s, r) = h(\tau(s, r))$, it remains to note that $\tau$ decreases in $x$ and increases in $y$:
	\[ \tau(x, y) - \tau(s, y) = \frac{(s-x)(1+y^2)}{(1+xy)(1+sy)} \geq 0, \qquad 
	\tau(s, y) - \tau(s, r) = \frac{(y-r)(1+s^2)}{(1+sy)(1+sr)} \geq 0. \]

label: thm-Rouche
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm-Rouche} (Rouch\'e) 
	Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}$ be a regular domain, and $f$, $g$ holomorphic on an open neighborhood of $\overline{\Omega}$ with $|f-g| < |f|$ on $\partial \Omega$.
	Then the number of zeroes of $f$ on $\Omega$, counted with multiplicity, is equal to that of $g$.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem-degree-2}
Let $\mathbf{A}$ be as in \Cref{prop-family-developingmaps-2}. Then there exists $\epsilon$ such that for all $u \in \mathbb{D}_\epsilon$, 
\[A_u: \mathcal{W}_u \rightarrow \mathbb{D}_{M'} \]  
is a branched double cover ramified exactly at $w = \pm 1$.

label: eqn-E(u)-bound
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $E(u) \coloneqq \underset{w \in \overline{\mathcal{B}}}{\sup} d\left( A_u(w), J(w) \right)$. 
By uniform convergence on $\overline{\mathcal{B}}$ (cf. \Cref{prop-family-developingmaps-2}), there exists $\epsilon$ such that for all $u \in \mathbb{D}_\epsilon$ we have 
\begin{equation}\label{eqn-E(u)-bound}
	E(u) < \min \left\{d(M', M), d(M, M+1), \frac{M-M'}{\kappa} \right\}, 
\qquad \kappa = \frac{1}{2}\left( 1 + (M+1)^2 \right).
\end{equation}
For a fixed $u \in \mathbb{D}_\epsilon$, we claim that
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
	\item $|A_u| > M'$ on $\overline{\mathcal{B}} \setminus \mathcal{A} = \mathcal{H} \sqcup \partial \mathcal{A}$;
	\item $|A_u| < M+1$ on $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$;
	\item $\underset{\overline{\mathcal{A}}}{\sup}|A_u - J| < M-M'$.
\end{enumerate}
To see (a), suppose that there exists $w \in \overline{\mathcal{B}} \setminus \mathcal{A}$ with $|A_u(w)| \leq M'$. 
Since $|J(w)| \geq M$, it follows from \Cref{lem-gap} that 
$d\left( A_u(w), J(w) \right) \geq d(M', M)$, which contradicts the bound \eqref{eqn-E(u)-bound}.
To see (b), suppose that there exists $w \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}$ with $|A_u(w)| \geq M+1$. Since $|J(w)| \leq M$, it follows again from \Cref{lem-gap} that $d\left( A_u(w), J(w) \right) \geq d(M, M+1)$, which contradicts the bound \eqref{eqn-E(u)-bound}.
To see (c), note that one can write
\[ |A_u - J| = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{(1+|A_u|^2) (1+ |J|^2)} \; d(A_u, J). \]
It follows from (b) that $|A_u - J| \leq \kappa \, d(A_u, J)$ on $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$. 
Part (c) now follows from the fact that we have chosen $\epsilon$ such that $d(A_u(w), J(w)) \leq E(u) < (M-M')/\kappa$ for all $w \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}$.  

Observe that it follows from (a) that $\mathcal{W}_u \subset \overline{\mathcal{W}_u} \subset \mathcal{A}$. 
Properness of the map $A_u: \mathcal{W}_u \rightarrow \mathbb{D}_{M'}$ follows from (a) and the compactness of $\overline{\mathcal{B}}$.
Indeed, let $K \subset \mathbb{D}_{M'}$ be compact. 
By (a), we have $A_u^{-1}(K) \cap \mathcal{W}_u = A_u^{-1}(K) \cap \overline{\mathcal{B}}$, which is a closed subset of $\overline{\mathcal{B}}$ and hence compact.
To compute the degree of $A_u$, for $\xi \in \mathbb{D}_{M'}$, let $f = J - \xi$ and $g = A_u - \xi$. On $\partial \mathcal{A}$ where $|J| = M$, we have
\[ |f - g| = |A_u - J| < M - M' < M - |\xi| = |J| - |\xi| \leq |J - \xi| = |f|. \]
By (b), $A_u$ has no poles near $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$, so $f$ and $g$ are holomorphic on a neighborhood of $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$.
We therefore can apply Rouch\'e Theorem \ref{thm-Rouche} to conclude that the number of preimages of $\xi$ via $A_u$ is equal to that via $J$ on $\mathcal{A}$, which is $2$ by \Cref{prop-Joukowsky}(i).
Since $\mathcal{W}_u = A_u^{-1}(\mathbb{D}_{M'}) \cap \mathcal{B} = A_u^{-1}(\mathbb{D}_{M'}) \cap \mathcal{A}$ by (a), the preimages of $\xi \in \mathbb{D}_{M'}$ in $\mathcal{A}$ are contained in $\mathcal{W}_u$. 
Finally, by continuity of $\mathbf{A}$ and since the branch locus of $A_0 = J$ is $J(\pm 1) = \pm 2$, 
we can further shrink $\epsilon$ if necessary to have $|A_u(\pm 1)| < M'$.
Then the ramification loci $\{ w = \pm 1 \} \subset \mathcal{A}$ are contained in $\mathcal{W}_u$. 
By construction of the family (\Cref{prop-family-developingmaps-1}), $A_u$ ramifies at $\pm 1$ and nowhere else.

title: Proof
body_md:
We consider the holomorphic family of developing maps in \Cref{prop-family-developingmaps-2} with $\epsilon$ given in \Cref{lem-degree-2}.
Fix nonzero $u \in \mathbb{D}_\epsilon$, and let $y_{u, \pm} \coloneqq A_u(\pm 1) \in \mathbb{D}_{M'}$ be the branch points of $A_u$.
Let $\overline{\gamma}_u$ be the straight segment connecting $y_{u, \pm}$: 
by construction, we have $\overline{\gamma}_u \subset \mathbb{D}_{M'}$.
Then the preimage $A_u^{-1}(\overline{\gamma}_u)$ consists of exactly two segments $\gamma_{u,1}$ and $\gamma_{u,2}$ that connect the critical points $w = \pm 1$
and develop to the same image $A_u(\gamma_{u,1}) = A_u(\gamma_{u,2}) = \overline{\gamma}_u$.

Let $\Delta_u$ be the bounded component of $\mathbb{C} \setminus (\gamma_{u,1} \cup \gamma_{u,2})$.
Then $\overline{\Delta_u} \subset \mathcal{B}$ and $A_u(\Delta_u) \subset \mathbb{P}^1 \setminus \overline{\gamma}_u$.
The map $A_u: \Delta_u \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^1 \setminus \overline{\gamma}_u$ is proper and a local homeomorphism, 
since $w = \pm 1$ are the only critical points of $A_u$ on $\mathbb{D}_R$. 
This means $\Delta_u$ is a covering of $\mathbb{P}^1 \setminus \overline{\gamma}_u$. 
Since both of these domains are connected and simply connected, $A_u$ must map $\Delta_u$ biholomorphically onto $\mathbb{P}^1 \setminus \overline{\gamma}_u$. 

We now recall that the coordinates change $z \rightarrow w = z/u$ is a M\" obius transform for nonzero $u$. 
In other words, $A_u(z/u)$ is a developing map of $\mathcal{D}_u$. 
Hence the images of $\gamma_{u,1}$ and $\gamma_{u,2}$ under the inverse M\" obius transform are twin paths connecting the apparent singularities $x_\pm$ of $\mathcal{D}_u$, bounding a disc that develops biholomorphically onto $\mathbb{P}^1 \setminus \overline{\gamma}_u$. 
Let $\sigma_u$ be the projective structure obtained from $\mathcal{D}_u$ by collapsing the disc $\Delta_u$, 
and $\gamma_u$ be the segment on $\sigma_u$ along which the two twin paths are glued, which develops onto $\overline{\gamma}_u$.
By \Cref{thm-twinpaths-bubble}, we have $\mathcal{D}_u = \mathrm{Bub}(\sigma_u, \gamma_u)$.
\qed

\begin{proof}
	This can be checked explicitly by plugging \eqref{eqn-form-B} and \eqref{eqn-form-D} in \eqref{linear-eqn-1}.
	Specifically, the coefficients at the orders $u^{-1}$ and $u^0$ of $\nu_\pm(u)$ ensure that $C_\pm(u)$ are regular at $u=0$, 
	while the coefficients at the order $u^1$ of $\nu_\pm(u)$ 
	together with part 1 of \Cref{lemma-linear-system-right-side} ensure that 
	$C_+(0) = C_-(0) = C_0$, where
	\begin{align}\label{limit-RHS}
		C_0 \coloneqq 
		\begin{cases}
			 -\nu' - \frac{3}{4} \underset{u \rightarrow 0}{\lim} \frac{1 }{u} R^{(1)}_{u,-}(u) 
			 &\text{ for } \nu_\pm(u) = \pm \frac{3}{4u} \pm \nu' u + \mathcal{O}(u^2), \\
			 -\nu_0^2 + \nu' - \frac{1}{4} \underset{u \rightarrow 0}{\lim} \frac{1}{u} R^{(1)}_{u, -}(u)
			 &\text{ for } \nu_\pm(u) = \mp \frac{1}{4u} + \nu_0 \pm \nu' u + \mathcal{O}(u^2).
		\end{cases}
	\end{align}
	Then the linear system \eqref{linear-system-total} limits to
	\begin{align}\label{linear-system-total-limit}
			&q_u^{(0)}(0) 
			= C_0, 
			&q_{u}^{(0)} (z_r(x_r)) 
			= - \nu_r(0)^2, 
	\end{align}
	for $3 \leq r \leq d$.
	Note that the dimension of $Q_{x_0 + \mathbf{x'}}$
	must have the minimal value $3g- 2 - d$
	since otherwise condition \eqref{condition-neighborhood} will be violated.
	This yields the rank $d-1$ of the system \eqref{linear-system-total-limit}.
\end{proof}

label: E1-E2
title: Proof
body_md:
\begin{proof}
We will make use of the representation \eqref{linear-system-decoupled} of \eqref{linear-system-total}
using a family $\mathbf{q}_{u} = \{ (q_{k, u})_{k = 1}^{3g-3} \}_{u \in z(U)}$ of basis of $H^0(K^2)$ 
constructed in \Cref{lemma-basis-of-quadratic-differentials}.
Let us use the basis corresponding to $u=0$ and expand $q = \sum_{k=1}^{3g-3} E^0_k q_{k, 0}$.
We need to show that there exist $\nu_\pm(u)$ of the prescribed forms such that the solutions to \eqref{linear-system-decoupled-1},
\begin{align}\label{E1-E2}
	&E_1(u) = \frac{C_+(u) q_2(-u) -  C_-(u) q_2(u)}{q_1(u) q_2(-u) -  q_1(-u) q_2(u)},
	&E_2(u) = \frac{ q_1(u) C_-(u)  -  q_1(-u) C_+(u)  }{q_1(u) q_2(-u) -  q_1(-u) q_2(u)},
\end{align}
where $C_\pm(u)$ are defined as in \eqref{linear-system-total},
have well-defined $u \rightarrow 0$ limits which are equal to $E_1^0$ and $E_2^0$ respectively.
To this end, denote by $N_1(u)$ and $N_2(u)$ the respective numerators in \eqref{E1-E2}.
Since $\underset{u\rightarrow 0}{\lim} C_\pm(u) = C_0$ (cf. \eqref{limit-RHS}), both $N_1(u)$ and $N_2(u)$ are holomorphic and vanish at $u = 0$.
Since the denominators of \eqref{E1-E2} have simple zero at $u=0$ by \Cref{lemma-basis-of-quadratic-differentials},
the $u\rightarrow 0$ limits of $E_1(u)$ and $E_2(u)$ are well-defined by L'Hôpital's rule.
These limits are determined by the coefficient at order $u^1$ of $N_1(u)$ and $N_2(u)$.
With $R^{(i)}_{u, \pm}(z) = \sum_{m,n} R^{(i)}_{m,n} (\pm u)^m z^n$, one can compute explicitly these coefficients to be
\begin{align*}
	N_1(u) &= \frac{q_2(0)}{2}\left[ -4 (\nu_{+,2} + \nu_{-,2}) 
	+ 3 \left( R^{(2)}_{0,1} - R^{(2)}_{1,0} + R^{(1)}_{2,0} - R^{(1)}_{1,1} + R^{(1)}_{0,2} \right) \right] u \nonumber \\
	& \hspace{6mm} + \frac{q_2'(0)}{2} \left( 4\nu_1 + 3 R^{(1)}_{1,0} - 3 R^{(1)}_{0,1} \right)u + \mathcal{O}(u^2),	 \nonumber \\
	N_2(u)  &= - \frac{q_1'(0)}{2} \left[ 4\nu_1 + 3 R^{(1)}_{1,0} - 3 R^{(1)}_{0,1} \right] u + \mathcal{O}(u^2)
\end{align*}
for the ansatz $\nu_\pm(u) = \pm \frac{3}{4u} \pm \nu_1 u + \nu_{\pm, 2}u^2 + \mathcal{O}(u^3)$,
and 
\begin{align*}
	N_1(u) &= -\frac{q_2(0)}{2} \left[ 8\nu_0 \nu_1 
	+ 4\nu_0 \left( R^{(1)}_{0,1} - R^{(1)}_{1,0} \right) 
	+ R^{(1)}_{2,0} - R^{(1)}_{1,1} + R^{(1)}_{2,0} 
	+ 3 R^{(2)}_{1,0} - 3 R^{(2)}_{0,1}  \right]u \nonumber \\
	&\hspace{6mm}
	+ \frac{q_2'(0)}{2} \left[ 4\nu_0^2 - 4\nu_1 + R^{(1)}_{0,1} - R^{(1)}_{1,0} \right]u +\mathcal{O}(u^2) \nonumber \\
	N_2(u)  &=  \frac{q_1'(0)}{2} \left( -4 \nu_0^2 + 4 \nu_1 - R^{(1)}_{0,1} + R^{(1)}_{1,0}  \right) u + \mathcal{O}(u^2)
\end{align*}
for the ansatz $\nu_\pm(u) = \mp \frac{1}{4u} + \nu_0 \pm \nu_1 u + \nu_{\pm, 2}u^2 + \mathcal{O}(u^3)$.

Since $q_2(0)$ and $q_1'(0)$ are non-zero, we can tune 
$(\nu_1, \nu_{\pm, 2})$ in the first case
and $(\nu_0, \nu_1)$ in the second case
to tune the coefficients of order $u^1$ of $N_1(u)$ and $N_2(u)$ as we want.
Hence there exist holomorphic functions $\nu_\pm(u): U\setminus \{x_0\} \rightarrow \mathbb C$ with the Laurent expansion at $u = 0$ of the form \eqref{eqn-form-B} or \eqref{eqn-form-D},
so that $\underset{u \rightarrow 0}{\lim} E_1(u) = E_1^0$ and $\underset{u \rightarrow 0}{\lim} E_2(u) = E_2^0$.
For $3 \leq r \leq d$, let $\nu_r \in \mathbb C$ be such that $E^0_{r} = -\nu_r^2$, and define $\nu_r(u) = \nu_r$ for all $u\in z(U)$.
The tuple $(E_1(u), E_2(u), E_3(u), ..., E_{3g-3}(u) ) = (E_1(u), E_2(u), E^0_3, ..., E^0_{3g-3})$ then defines for each $u \neq 0$ a holomorphic quadratic differential $q^{(0)}_u \coloneqq \sum_{k=1}^{3g-3} E_k(u) q_{k,u}$
that solves the linear system \eqref{linear-system-decoupled} 
defined by $(\nu_\pm(u), \nu_3(u), ..., \nu_d(u))$,
with $\underset{u \rightarrow 0}{\lim} q^{(0)}_u = q$ a solution to the corresponding limit linear system \eqref{linear-system-total-limit}.
\end{proof}

Since $q_2(0)$ and $q_1'(0)$ are non-zero, we can tune 
$(\nu_1, \nu_{\pm, 2})$ in the first case
and $(\nu_0, \nu_1)$ in the second case
to tune the coefficients of order $u^1$ of $N_1(u)$ and $N_2(u)$ as we want.

so that $\underset{u \rightarrow 0}{\lim} E_1(u) = E_1^0$ and $\underset{u \rightarrow 0}{\lim} E_2(u) = E_2^0$.

The tuple $(E_1(u), E_2(u), E_3(u), ..., E_{3g-3}(u) ) = (E_1(u), E_2(u), E^0_3, ..., E^0_{3g-3})$ then defines for each $u \neq 0$ a holomorphic quadratic differential $q^{(0)}_u \coloneqq \sum_{k=1}^{3g-3} E_k(u) q_{k,u}$
that solves the linear system \eqref{linear-system-decoupled} 
defined by $(\nu_\pm(u), \nu_3(u), ..., \nu_d(u))$,
with $\underset{u \rightarrow 0}{\lim} q^{(0)}_u = q$ a solution to the corresponding limit linear system \eqref{linear-system-total-limit}.

\begin{proof}
	We will show explicitly that,
	as a multi-variable function with variables $u$ and $z$,
	\eqref{family-merom-q-db} limits to \eqref{q_x_0-local-form} as $u \rightarrow 0$.
	To this end, it suffices to show that given any $z \neq 0$,
	the $u \rightarrow 0$ limit of the evaluation of \eqref{family-merom-q-db} at $z$ 
	is the evaluation of \eqref{q_x_0-local-form} at $z$.	
	Plugging $\nu_{\pm}(u) = \mp \frac{1}{4u} + \nu_0 \pm \nu' u + \mathcal{O}(u^2)$ into \eqref{family-merom-q-db}
	yields
	\begin{align}\label{plug-in-db}
		\frac{-2z^2 - u^2}{(z-u)^2 (z+u)^2} 
		+ \frac{2\nu_0 z}{(z-u)(z+u)}
		- \frac{R^{(1)}_{u,+}(z) - R^{(1)}_{u,-}(z) }{ 4u }
		+ \nu_0 \left( R^{(1)}_{u,+}(z) + R^{(1)}_{u,-}(z) \right) & \nonumber \\
		 - \frac{3}{4} \left( R^{(2)}_{u,+}(z) + R^{(2)}_{u,-}(z) \right)
		+ \mathcal{O}(u)(z) &.
	\end{align}
	Here we have ignored the factor $dz^2$
	and denoted by $\mathcal{O}(u)(z)$ a function with variables $u$ and $z$ such that,
	given any $z' \neq 0$,
	the function $F_{z'}(u) \coloneqq \mathcal{O}(u)(z) \mid_{z = z'}$ is holomorphic on $\{ u \mid 0 \leq |u| \leq |z'|/2 \}$
	with $F_{z'}(u) \sim \mathcal{O}(u)$.
	It follows that $\underset{u \rightarrow 0}{\lim} \mathcal{O}(u)(z) = \mathcal{O}(u)(z)\mid_{u = 0}$, 
	which a priori defines a function in $z$,
	is the zero function. 
	By a similar argument, we can take the $u \rightarrow 0$ limit of the other terms in \eqref{plug-in-db} explicitly 
	and obtain $q^{(2)}_{x_0}$ as in \eqref{q_x_0-local-form} as the limit.
	
	To show that $q^{(2)}_{x_0}$ is holomorphic on $C \setminus \{x_0\}$, it suffices to show holomorphicity on $C\setminus U$.
	Given $p\in C\setminus U$ and a coordinate neighborhood $(V,w)$ of $p$, 
	let $q^{(i)}_{u,\pm}(w) dw^2$ be the local form of $q^{(i)}_{u,\pm}$ on $V$.
	We want to show that the evaluation of \eqref{family-merom-q-db} at $p$, which defines the function
	\begin{align}\label{evaluation-at-p}
		\sum_{s\in \{\pm\}} \nu_s(u) q^{(1)}_{u, s}(w(p)) - \frac{3}{4} \sum_{s\in \{\pm\}} q^{(2)}_{u, s}(w(p))
		= \frac{1}{4u}\left( -q^{(1)}_{u,+}(w(p)) + q^{(1)}_{u,-} (w(p))  \right) + \mathcal{O}(1)
	\end{align}
	in $u$ which is holomorphic at $u \neq 0$
	has a well-defined $u \rightarrow 0$ limit.
	Since $q^{(i)}_{u,\pm} \overset{u \rightarrow 0}{\rightarrow} q^{(i)}_0$, 
	which is holomorphic on $C \setminus \{x_0\}$,
	it suffices to show that the leading term $\frac{1}{4u}\left( -q^{(1)}_{u,+}(w(p)) + q^{(1)}_{u,-} (w(p))  \right)$
	of \eqref{evaluation-at-p} has a well-defined $u \rightarrow 0$ limit.
	This is achieved by an argument similar to the proof of part 2 of \Cref{lemma-linear-system-right-side}.
	Furthermore, for $p \in \{x_3, ..., x_d\}$, since \eqref{evaluation-at-p} vanishes for $u\neq 0$, it is identically zero for all $u \in z(U)$.	
\end{proof}

	\[ -\frac{3}{4}\left[ \frac{1}{(z-u)^2} + \frac{1}{(z+u)^2} \right] + \frac{3}{4u}\left[ \frac{1}{z-u} - \frac{1}{z+u} \right] + \mathcal{O}(u)

	which tends to $0$ for every fixed $z \neq 0$, instead of to $-2/z^2$ as in \eqref{plug-in-db}.
	Hence the limit \eqref{delta-q} has no pole at $x_0$, and it is holomorphic on $U$ by \Cref{lemma-linear-system-right-side}.
